input.lesson_title: When a variable stops being valid
input.lesson_objective: Be able to predict whether a Rust variable is still usable after an assignment.
input.question: Explain in 2-3 sentences why, after `let b = a;` with `a` of type `String`, you can no longer use `a`.
input.rubric:
Expected key points (essential: 1 and 2):
1. The String value was moved into `b`: ownership passes to `b`.
2. Every value has a single owner, so `a` is no longer valid/usable after the move.
3. (secondary) The compiler reports it at compile time, or for Copy types like i32 the variable stays valid instead.
Typical mistakes: "the string is copied and `a` stays valid" (thinks assignment always copies); "`a` is deleted/zeroed" (thinks of an emptied value).
Partial answer: says the value moves into `b` but does not explain why `a` is no longer usable (the single owner is missing), or the reverse.
Tone of the feedback: support, say what is missing, never judge.
input.answer: Cause with that line the value of the string goes to `b`, i mean b becomes the owner. In rust theres only one owner at a time so `a` isnt valid anymore and the compiler gives me an error.

rubric.text: The feedback says concretely what the answer shows (the value goes to `b`, a single owner).
It does not invent gaps or demand details the rubric does not ask for.
No explicit praise and no grade.

cases.description: English version: a precise wrong belief (assignment copies the string). Must grade `incorrect` and name the misconception in the third person.

input.answer: Actually `a` can still be used, because `let b = a;` makes a copy of the string, so there are two identical strings.

rubric.text: `misconception` says the person thinks assignment copies the String (third person, one sentence).
The feedback acknowledges, anywhere, why the belief seems reasonable (in other languages/types it works that way) and explains the move.
The feedback gives the correct idea (move, single owner, `a` no longer valid).
It does not judge the person.
The feedback speaks directly to the person ("you", "you expected", "It seems you think...") with a supportive tone, not in an impersonal form.
